questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$. What does the constraint $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ express for a fixed plant $i$?
options: Centre $i$ receives in total at most the capacity $s_i$
Each single route from plant $i$ carries at most $s_i$
Plant $i$ ships at most $s_i$ in total over all centres
Plant $i$ must produce exactly its capacity $s_i$

questions.question: In a transportation problem with plant capacities $s_i$ and required deliveries $d_j$, total capacity $\sum_is_i=90$ exceeds total demand $\sum_jd_j=75$. A modeller writes the plant constraints as $\sum_jx_{ij}=s_i$ and the demand constraints as $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$. What goes wrong?
options: Nothing: equality simply makes every plant use its full capacity
It is infeasible: 90 units must ship but only 75 can be delivered
The optimum now ships 15 extra units on the cheapest available route
The model becomes unbounded, since 15 units have no destination

questions.question: In a transportation problem minimizing $\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$ with all unit costs $c_{ij}>0$, shipments $x_{ij}\ge0$ and plant constraints $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$, the demand constraints are wrongly written as $\sum_ix_{ij}\le d_j$. What is the optimal plan?
options: Ship exactly $d_j$ to every centre $j$
Ship nothing at all, with total cost 0
Ship each plant's full capacity $s_i$
Ship only on the single cheapest route

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$, where all $s_i$ and $d_j$ are integers and the model is feasible. Why do the shipments not need integrality restrictions to get a whole-unit plan?
options: Every feasible shipment plan is automatically integer-valued
Shipments are continuous, so whole units are never relevant
An optimal plan with integer shipments always exists anyway
Integer unit costs $c_{ij}$ force the shipments to be integers

questions.question: A transportation model minimizes $\sum_i\sum_jc_{ij}x_{ij}$, where $x_{ij}\ge0$ is the amount shipped from plant $i$ to centre $j$. A haulier also charges a fixed fee of 500 for every route that is used at all. Can this objective represent that fee?
options: No; it only charges cost proportional to each amount shipped
Yes; the fee is absorbed by adding 500 to each unit cost $c_{ij}$
Yes; the fee is constant, so it does not change the optimal plan
No; fixed fees make the model infeasible whatever is shipped

questions.question: A transportation problem has 3 plants and 4 centres, one shipment variable $x_{ij}$ per plant-centre route, one capacity constraint per plant and one demand constraint per centre. How many shipment variables and capacity/demand constraints does it have?
options: 12 variables and 7 constraints
7 variables, one per location, and 12 constraints
12 variables and 12 constraints
7 variables and 7 constraints

questions.question: A transportation problem has unit costs $c_{11}=5$, $c_{12}=3$, $c_{21}=2$, $c_{22}=6$ (plant $i$, centre $j$). Plant 1 ships 10 units to centre 1 and 20 to centre 2; plant 2 ships 15 units to centre 1 and nothing to centre 2. What is the total transport cost?

Two plants with capacities $s_1=40$, $s_2=30$ supply two centres with required deliveries $d_1=25$, $d_2=35$. Plans list $(x_{11},x_{12};x_{21},x_{22})$, where $x_{ij}$ is shipped from plant $i$ to centre $j$. Which plan is feasible?
A transportation problem has two plants and two centres, with $x_{ij}$ the amount shipped from plant $i$ to centre $j$. Which constraint states that centre 2 receives exactly its required 35 units?

Two plants have capacities 40 and 30; three centres require 25 units each. Every plant can ship to every centre; capacities are upper bounds and deliveries must be exact. What can be said about feasibility?
options: Infeasible, as total capacity 70 is below total demand 75
Feasible, as each plant's capacity exceeds every single demand
Feasible, as the plant capacities are only upper bounds
Feasible, as only 5 units of demand would go undelivered

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$. Total capacity equals total demand, $\sum_is_i=\sum_jd_j$. What holds for every feasible plan?
options: Every plant ships exactly its capacity $s_i$
Every route carries the same amount of goods
Some plant must keep unused capacity
Every plant ships to every centre

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$, and all $c_{ij}>0$. Suppose the demand constraints are relaxed to $\sum_ix_{ij}\ge d_j$. Why does this not improve the optimal cost?
options: Over-delivery never happens, as plant capacities rule it out
The relaxed model is infeasible, so its optimum cannot be compared
The relaxed model always over-delivers, which raises cost instead
Shipments into an over-supplied centre can be cut back, saving cost

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$. The route from plant 2 to centre 3 is closed by a road block. How should the model be changed?
options: Set $c_{23}=0$, so the route has no effect
Add $x_{23}=0$ or drop the variable $x_{23}$
Delete the capacity constraint of plant 2
Set $d_3=0$, since centre 3 cannot be served

questions.question: In a transportation problem with plant capacities 30 and 20 and centre demands 25 and 25 (balanced), the optimal plan costs 190. Every unit cost on routes out of plant 1 rises by 2. What is the new minimum cost?

Plant 1 (capacity 50) and plant 2 (capacity 20) supply centre 1 (30 units) and centre 2 (35 units). Unit costs: $c_{11}=3$, $c_{12}=5$, $c_{21}=4$, $c_{22}=2$. In the cost-minimizing plan, which plant has unused capacity, and how much?
options: Plant 1, with 20 units unused
Plant 2, with 20 units unused
Neither plant has unused capacity
Plant 1, with 5 units left unused

questions.question: Plants 1 and 2 have capacities 30 and 40; centres 1 and 2 require 35 each, so total capacity equals total demand. The route from plant 2 to centre 1 is closed. What can be concluded?
options: A feasible plan exists, since total capacity equals demand
A feasible plan exists if plant 1 ships 35 to centre 1
No feasible plan exists, as centre 1 can get at most 30
A feasible plan exists, as plant 2 can cover centre 2 alone

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$. All $s_i$ and $d_j$ are integers, the model is feasible, and an LP solver returns an optimal plan. Must this plan have integer shipments?
options: Yes; integer supplies and demands make every optimal plan integral
Yes, provided that the unit costs $c_{ij}$ are integers as well
No; some optimum is integral, but ties allow fractional optima too
No; integer supplies and demands give fractional optima in general

questions.question: A transportation problem ships $x_{ij}\ge0$ units from plant $i$ (capacity $s_i$) to centre $j$ (demand $d_j$) at unit cost $c_{ij}$: minimize $\sum_{i,j}c_{ij}x_{ij}$ s.t. $\sum_jx_{ij}\le s_i$ for all $i$, $\sum_ix_{ij}=d_j$ for all $j$. A subsidy makes $c_{12}=-1$; all other costs are positive. If the demands are relaxed to $\sum_ix_{ij}\ge d_j$, how does the optimum compare with the original?
options: It is the same, since $\ge$ demand never improves a transport plan
It is the same, since the subsidy is too small to change any plan
It is infeasible, since negative costs violate nonnegativity
It can be cheaper, by shipping surplus units along route (1,2)

questions.question: Plants with capacities 40 and 30 supply centres needing 20, 30 and 20. Unit costs: plant 1: 4, 2, 6; plant 2: 8, 1, 3 (to centres 1, 2, 3). Filling the cheapest remaining route first gives cost 230. What is the minimum cost?

Plants 1 and 2 (capacity 40 each) supply centres 1 and 2 (30 each). Unit costs are 2 and 3 from plant 1 and 3 and 4 from plant 2 (to centres 1 and 2); the minimum cost is 170. All plant-1 costs rise by 3. What is the new minimum cost?
